A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by Datar and Ay. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical simulations of gradient flows, including measured convergence rates over 100 random initializations in Section 3 and Figures 2–4.

after.justification: v2 retains those simulations and adds higher-dimensional experiments and finite-sample full-batch and stochastic optimization results, including Tables 1–2.

M1.justification: The original GD/NGD framework and Fisher geometry remain unchanged. Section 5 adds empirical-target and mini-batch stochastic adaptations, with explicit update equations and a decaying learning rate, rather than replacing the underlying method.

E1.justification: The task remains KL minimization over synthetic discrete distributions. Section 5 adds a target-access scenario in which optimization uses finite observations rather than exact target probabilities; no real-world dataset or separate application domain is introduced.

E2.justification: The comparisons retain Euclidean gradient methods in η and θ coordinates against natural gradient, including their corresponding stochastic versions. K-FAC appears only in future-work discussion and is not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds n = 10 simulations and finite-sample discrete-time protocols, including full-batch and mini-batch updates. Section 5 compares equal small learning rates with individually tuned rates and measures convergence by the maximum iterations across 100 initializations to a fixed tolerance. These are new protocols, not documented reruns of the retained continuous-time experiments.

E4.justification: Figures 9 and 11 add substantial learning-rate sensitivity analyses for full-batch and stochastic optimization, testing when NGD's advantage emerges. Figures 6–7 also examine whether the convergence ordering persists at higher dimension. The earlier curvature analysis and nonconvexity counterexample are retained, with the latter relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report variation across 100 random initializations, and v2 extends this convention to additional experiments. Neither introduces seed identifiers, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a new uncertainty-reporting practice. The new maximum-iteration statistic serves as a performance metric rather than an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: The original n = 2 convergence findings remain. New n = 10 flow results report rates approximately 16.239, 0.099, and 1.974 for η-GD, θ-GD, and NGD. Under the newly tuned empirical settings, Table 1 reports 29, 12, and 2 iterations respectively; Table 2 reports 41, 20, and 3 for stochastic updates. These are added results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 materially revises assumptions and proofs. Theorem 7 requires a uniform perturbation margin below 1, correcting v1 Theorem 4.3's pointwise bound. Appendix A's Theorem 9 restricts v1's arbitrary-initialization reverse-KL result to sufficiently small initial divergence and replaces its global argument with local reasoning. Theorem 3's proof also revises the compactness argument and explicitly establishes the local T = 0 case. Other proofs are largely relocated.

C1.justification: The abstract's central convergence-ordering and conditioning claims remain. A fourth introductory contribution and the expanded conclusion extend the claims to finite-sample full-batch and stochastic settings, distinguishing NGD superiority with tuned rates from sandwich ordering with equal small rates.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability qualifications: the unknown transient before asymptotic bounds apply, local versus nonlinear discrete-time behavior, and exact versus approximate Fisher information. Section 4.1 corrects the perturbation interpretation from the Fisher matrix to its inverse. The conclusion adds a conditional route toward K-FAC guarantees and discusses the limits of extending the results beyond the simplex.

D1.justification: The new experiments document empirical-frequency target construction, uniform mini-batch sampling, a learning-rate decay formula, and numerical learning rates in Tables 1–2. Reproducibility remains limited because the dataset size, batch size, stopping tolerance, and decay parameter are unspecified; no code or data access information is added.

R1.justification: Bullo's Lectures on Network Systems is removed together with the LaSalle-based argument in Appendix A. The remaining cited works and principal research positioning are retained; venue and bibliographic updates do not represent new references.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: main-text proofs move into Appendix C, the former nonconvexity appendix moves into Section 3, and references precede the appendices. Explanations of convergence and limitations expand, and a dedicated empirical section is inserted before the conclusion.

P2.justification: The five original figures are retained and rearranged, including the nonconvexity plot becoming Figure 2. v2 adds Figures 6–12 and three tables covering higher-dimensional behavior, empirical trajectories, learning-rate sensitivity, and theory–experiment correspondence. Typography, captions, and page layout are also extensively reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important theoretical deficiencies through the uniform stability margin in Theorem 7 and the appropriately restricted reverse-KL theorem in Appendix A. The new experiments directly test learning-rate-dependent comparisons in finite-sample and stochastic settings, while expanded limitations clarify what the theory establishes. These provide substantial gains in rigor and evidential support, although the experiments remain synthetic and incompletely specified for reproduction.
